tagline: Sandstone pockets, a mining townsite and a sinkhole on a rugged loop
intro: Gold Butte Back Country Byway makes a rugged, 62-mile loop through southern Nevada. The Bureau of Land Management identifies it as one of the first designated backcountry byways, offering sandstone formations, rock carvings, sinkholes and views toward Lake Mead and Valley of Fire. Allow four to five hours for the drive.

The loop passes the former mining town of Gold Butte, where a gold discovery in 1905 brought a rush of people in 1905 and 1906. Prospectors also worked mica, magnesite, copper and zinc, but no significant deposits were found. By December 1910, most mining had stopped and the town was abandoned. In 2016, President Barack Obama established Gold Butte National Monument after a campaign by conservation groups, lawmakers and the Moapa Band of Paiute Indians.

From State Route 170, Gold Butte Road heads into the national monument and reaches Whitney Pocket, where the pavement ends. Graded native soil continues for approximately 20 miles to the townsite. There the route turns north on Gold Butte Wash Road, narrows to one lane and continues to Mud Wash. Mud Wash Road leads to Devil's Throat; just beyond the sinkhole, the byway rejoins Gold Butte Road.

moments.title: Whitney Pocket
moments.text: At Whitney Pocket, water and wind have worked a sandstone wall into pockets of different sizes over millennia. This is also where the pavement ends. The next stretch toward Gold Butte townsite runs on graded native soil for approximately 20 miles.
moments.notice: Look for the differently sized pockets eroded into the sandstone wall.

moments.title: Gold Butte townsite
moments.text: Gold Butte's surviving traces are spare: a couple of foundations, two graves and several old mine shafts. The mountain above the town reaches 5,013 feet. The 1905 gold discovery brought a rush of people that continued into 1906. The settlement acquired a post office, hotel, livery stable, store and homes. Yet the entire mining district produced $75,000, and no significant deposits were found. By December 1910 the town was abandoned, with most mining halted. The ghost town and the nearby peak now lie within Gold Butte National Monument, managed by the Bureau of Land Management.

moments.title: Devil's Throat
moments.text: Devil's Throat is a 110-foot sinkhole along the byway. On the return from Gold Butte townsite, Mud Wash Road begins in a wide wash and leads to the sinkhole. Just past it, the loop meets Gold Butte Road at approximately mile 29.

practical: Whitney Pocket: The rugged loop requires sturdy tires and a high-clearance vehicle, especially for the final 20 miles on Gold Butte Wash Road and Mud Wash Road. (checked 2026-10-11)
